data.title: These baby names are popular in one state and one state only: Data
data.description:
(NEXSTAR) – Odds are high that, if you’ve had a child in the last seven years, their name is Olivia or Liam. And if it isn’t, there’s a good chance they have a friend or classmate with either name. 

Olivia and Liam remained the most popular baby names for girls and boys, respectively, in 2025, marking the seventh consecutive year that the combo has remained at the top of the Social Security Administration’s list. 

The nation’s most popular baby names have hardly changed in recent years. Since 2020, the same three names have ranked among the top five for girls – Oliva, Charlotte, and Emma – and boys – Liam, Noah, and Oliver. 

At least one of those names ranked as the most popular in all but three states. Hawaii’s most popular baby names in 2025 were Elijah and Isla. James and Amelia topped their respective charts in Mississippi, and in Wyoming, it was Theodore and Aurora that came out on top. 

For what it’s worth, even all of those have ranked among the most popular in the nation since 2020 – the lowest-ranked overall is Isla, coming in at No. 44 once.

There are some names, however, that ranked as the most popular in some states despite not cracking into the nation’s top 100 at all since 2020. 

An analysis by Nexstar found that, between 2020 and 2025 (the most recent data available from the Social Security Administration), Declan ranked among the top 100 boy names in 38 states at least once. If you look at the most popular names in the country overall, the highest the name has ever ranked over the same period is No. 102.

Among girls, Parker was among the hottest names in 36 states at least once since 2020. The name peaked at No. 106 across all girl names in the U.S. last year. 

But there are names popular in one state and one state only. Some have never even cracked into the top 1,000 names in the U.S.

Between 2020 and 2025, Hawaii had the greatest number of trending names unique to its state. That includes 22 names that have never ranked among the top in the nation.

In total, 23 states and the District of Columbia had at least one girls’ name that was popular nowhere else. Among boy names, 21 states and DC saw at least one unique option. 

Some may be on the verge of becoming popular elsewhere. Milan, which recently spiked in popularity in Florida, has ranked among the top 300 names in the U.S. since 2023. Milani, popular only in Delaware, first broke into the United States’ top 1,000 girls’ names in 2014 and has been trending upward since. 

Saint, a name that has only trended in the District of Columbia as of late, ranked at No. 267 in the U.S. last year, a huge jump since breaking into the top 1,000 in 2018. 

Lottie, one of Wyoming’s most popular names, returned to the nation’s top names in 2022 – a list it hadn’t been on since 1959. Last year, it was the 528th most common name among newborn girls.

It’s too soon to say whether Saint, Lottie, or any of the names in the above table will rank among the nation’s most popular anytime soon. 

There were more than 3 million babies born in 2025, though, so there’s a decent chance any of these names could appear on newly printed Social Security cards this year.

data.title: More discrimination among expectant moms is a bad prescription
data.description:
Weeks before her due date, first-time mother Erica Jimenez sought help with her pregnancy. Yet Jimenez was excluded from California’s Black Infant Health Program because she was not the right race.

When Jimenez attempted to access the program, a representative told her that the program was not for her and offered to show her other resources. Except for Jimenez’s race, she satisfied all the criteria that the organization presented: She was pregnant, she resided in an area that the program serves and she was over the age of 18.

Jimenez is now challenging Black Infant Health’s race-based eligibility for violating the equal protection clause of the Constitution’s 14th Amendment, which forbids the government from treating individuals differently based on race without a compelling interest.

Since 1989, California has implemented the Black Infant Health Program to improve the health of African American women, infants, and children by providing services exclusively to pregnant and postpartum Black women.

Those efforts seem to have failed. Despite more than three decades of Black Infant Health’s implementation, recent data show the mortality rate for Black infants remain higher than that of white infants.

So, after decades of race-based care, the problem persists. Yet California wants to continue the exact same treatment plan. A recent op-ed in The Hill criticized Jiminez’s lawsuit, implying there is nothing wrong with doing the same thing over and over and expecting a different result.

The piece states that aligning a public maternal health program with the Constitution and preventing it from discriminating by race is wrong because “paying attention to race in healthcare delivery can quite literally save lives.” That obviously is not what is happening in Black Infant Health. And all the while, California continues to deny Jimenez and other mothers like her equal treatment in the name of a benefit the program has failed to deliver.

While saving the lives of mothers and infants is certainly important, it doesn’t automatically justify governments use of disparate treatment by race and should continue to be viewed with skepticism. That is because our Constitution’s prohibition on racial discrimination recognizes our nation’s tragic history with race, including in the offering of separate but equal medical care.

Throughout American history, governments have repeatedly evoked the language of public health, medicine, and life-saving necessity to defend racial classifications. The Constitution does not permit the government to withhold equal treatment simply because it accompanies its discriminatory policies with an appeal to health or safety. Thus, declaring that something “saves lives” is not enough to maintain discrimination. Otherwise, the government could maintain any discriminatory program on the broad and tenuous assertion that it saves lives.

The Supreme Court has therefore repeatedly rejected broad, aspirational objectives — whether promoting diversity, serving a child’s interests in a custody dispute, or remedying societal discrimination — as too amorphous to justify racial discrimination. California’s asserted interest in reducing health disparities is no different.

Moreover, the Constitution does not permit California to continue a discriminatory program that disadvantages and stereotypes individuals like Jimenez on the basis of race. Indeed, the fundamental eligibility criteria to participate in Black Infant Health is based on race. 

The story waves the bloody shirt of saving mothers and babies to decry efforts to eliminate discrimination as “cruel.” But what is truly cruel is treating mothers and their infants based on their skin color rather than their need. As Justice Clarence Thomas noted, “Every time the government places citizens on racial registers and makes race relevant to the provisions of burdens or benefits, it demeans us all.”

And Jimenez’s lawsuit does not seek to exclude any mother from the program on the basis of race. Instead, Jimenez wants all moms who meet the criteria to be able to access the program, regardless of race. It is California and its defenders who want to preserve a form of exclusion that history long ago rejected.

Nonetheless, Black Infant Health Program’s potential to save the lives of mothers and their infants through racially segregated care is doubtful, given its demonstrated ineffectiveness over the last three decades.

The story cites a study in Florida showing that mortality of Black infants was reduced when they were treated by Black care providers. But that study was substantially undermined in a follow-up review using the same data set. The original study had been driven by omitted-variable bias, as white physicians disproportionately treated the highest-risk newborns, which were the ones with extremely low birth weight. The evidence thus no longer supports the claim of physician-patient racial concordance.

The better care plan for California’s moms is the same one that The Constitution prescribes: individual treatment. As the Supreme Court reiterated in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard, “Government must treat citizens as individuals,” not as mere components of a racial class. The same goes for health care. As William Osler, the Father of Modern Medicine, stated, “The good physician treats the disease; the great physician treats the patient who has the disease.”

Good medicine does not cling to failed treatments. It changes course. California’s approach to maternal and infant health does the opposite, persisting with a remedy that is not only ineffective but also unlawful.

Andrew Quinio is an attorney at Pacific Legal Foundation and is representing Erica Jimenez in her lawsuit against the State of California.

data.title: Canada announces retaliatory tariffs to begin Sept. 8
data.description:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Saturday morning that the country will enact retaliatory tariffs on the U.S. beginning on Sept. 8 in response to the Trump administration’s new 50 percent tariffs. 

The prime minister said during a press conference that the country will “match Washington’s new tariffs dollar for dollar in order to protect Canadian workers, farmers, families and businesses.”

Carney said his government will release more details about these retaliatory policies in the “coming days” and that the tariffs would apply to goods like steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics. 

He stressed during his morning remarks that the Canadian government “take[s] this step reluctantly.”

“Reluctantly because we recognize that some of these measures will raise costs and reduce choice for Canadians,” Carney said. “Reluctantly because we recognize that some U.S. companies and some U.S. states are innocent bystanders in a dispute that they did not want. Reluctantly because this trade dispute is preventing Canada and America from doing so much good that we could do together. 

“But at the same time, we take this step confident that it is in the best interest of Canada,” the prime minister added.

The new U.S. tariffs, which went into effect at midnight, impose a 50 percent tariff on over $20 billion worth of Canadian goods. This impacts a wide range of imported products, from wine to hockey sticks to cement.  

In a statement released earlier in the day, Carney announced that he had instructed Canadian negotiators to walk away from these trade negotiations on Friday evening, just hours before the new U.S. policies went into effect.

Carney said he made this decision after U.S. negotiators introduced new terms at the last minute. 

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer pushed back on this characterization of these talks in a statement shared on social media. 

“Despite the U.S. offer to Canada to receive the best treatment of any major exporter to our market, new demands and walk backs of other commitments by Canada have upended the careful balance reached in the past days,” he wrote, calling this a “missed opportunity” for an economic partnership between the two countries.

data.title: Across the country, Kennedy touts MAHA, but not vaccines
data.description:
Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. stood in the Oval Office last week as President Trump proudly signed an executive order to reduce childhood vaccines, heavily implying a link between vaccines and autism. 

But when Kennedy made appearances in California and then hit the campaign trail for Republicans in Iowa over the past week, vaccines weren’t on the agenda at all. 

In Iowa, he spoke on the importance of nutrition, youth fitness and the revived presidential fitness test with Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R-Iowa) at a YMCA. 

“We think the sedentary condition of many of our children is contributing to this malaise, to the mental health crisis, to the physical fitness crisis, to the chronic disease crisis in our country,” Kennedy said. 

Alongside Republican Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds, Kennedy announced a new statewide addiction treatment and prevention program. He visited a community health center to participate in a roundtable discussion focused on expanding access to primary and preventive care.

Kennedy even went fishing with Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn, who has been endorsed by Kennedy’s Make America Healthy Again PAC.  

Through all his events over the past week, Kennedy has addressed vaccination — and by extension the country’s measles epidemic — only when asked a direct question.  

“We’re doing everything that we can,” Kennedy told reporters in Dubuque, Iowa, about measles, saying the U.S. is in much better shape than other countries. 

He blamed the COVID-19 pandemic for a loss of faith in the public health system and declining vaccinations worldwide, without mentioning the new executive order. 

“During COVID, people lost faith in the public health system. … My job is to make the public health establishment trustworthy,” Kennedy said.

He is in the middle of a 10-day swing across Iowa, Minnesota and Florida, the White House said, part of his sweeping Make America Healthy Again Tour aimed at keeping MAHA supporters engaged ahead of the midterm elections.  

It’s a sign the administration views Kennedy as an important asset in trying to help Republicans keep control of government. 

“No administration has done more to address America’s chronic disease epidemic than the Trump administration, from overhauling the Dietary Guidelines for Americans to removing artificial ingredients from our food supply,” White House spokesperson Kush Desai said in a statement to The Hill. 

“Secretary Kennedy and the entire HHS [Health and Human Services] team have been instrumental in these successes, and he will continue touting these historic wins for the American people.” 

But Kennedy’s localized messaging highlights the conundrum facing the administration on vaccination and the varied interests of MAHA voters who are not necessarily strong Republican primary midterm voters and don’t necessarily support Trump at all costs. 

The MAHA movement, which came about from the political alliance between Kennedy and Trump, is broadly focused on issues like chronic disease and childhood illness. It has elevated issues such as vaccine safety but also corporate interests in federal agencies and the presence of chemical additives and pesticides in the food supply.  

“I think that the MAHA agenda has been one of the highest priorities of this administration, and it hasn’t been isolated to one or two issues. It’s really been a pretty big breadth of policy issues that they’ve taken on and had success with,” said David Mansdoerfer, who served in the HHS during the first Trump administration.  

Mansdoerfer said he doesn’t think Kennedy is “shying away” from talking about vaccines so much as trying to sell what the administration says are MAHA wins. 

“’Whether you agree or disagree with us, we are delivering on the agenda that we promised.’ So, to me, [Kennedy’s appearances are] an opportunity to translate the policy efforts done in D.C. to the local level,” Mansdoerfer said.  

The White House and Kennedy had stepped back in recent months from aggressive actions to remake vaccine policy ahead of the midterms, until Trump brought it roaring back to the fore with his executive order aimed at reducing the number of recommended vaccines for the youngest children. 

During the Oval Office event, both Kennedy and Trump multiple times hinted at the debunked idea that rising rates of childhood shots have led to an increase in autism diagnoses.  

“Genes don’t cause epidemics. You need an environmental toxin,” Kennedy said, while thanking Trump for allowing him to reexamine the childhood immunization schedules.  

“Decades ago, children received only a small fraction of the vaccines required today. In those times, people were much healthier, and of course, the high rates of autism now observed did not exist,” Trump said. “So there’s a reason for such epidemic rates of autism, and we’re going to bring it back to where it was.”

But 24 hours later, Kennedy arrived in California, where he spent the next three days talking up substance abuse treatment and the administration’s faith-based solutions to addiction and homelessness.

Kennedy also spoke about combatting health fraud — a key priority for the Trump administration.

During a visit to a community health center in the Central Valley, Kennedy was asked about how the vaccine order would impact California.

“The president’s executive order should not change the way that children are vaccinated. In California, the state decides what the vaccination schedule is,” Kennedy said, as first reported by Politico.

data.title: Tuesday's election results could spell real trouble for Florida Republicans
data.description:
There was a political earthquake in Florida on Tuesday evening that could create prediction-shifting tremors — not only up until the midterm elections, but right through the 2028 presidential election. That earthquake was personified by far-left Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon (D), who absolutely crushed Alex Vindman, the Democratic Party’s sanctioned and favored candidate. 

The morning after, while I was still trying to wrap my mind around the shocking upset, I came across a piece from RealClearPolitics titled: “Florida Democrats Hand Republicans a November Gift.” I believe the message of the headline is way off the mark. For me — and for several Republican operatives I spoke with this week — Nixon’s decisive victory represents a neon red warning sign for Florida Republicans. 

In recent years, many pundits have claimed Florida to be “deep red” politically. I don’t believe that to be the case. I do believe Gov. Ron DeSantis has proven himself to be an exceptional governor, saving the state from the draconian dictates rolled out during the COVID-19 pandemic. But unfortunately for the Republican Party, DeSantis is not on the ballot in November. Neither is his highly capable wife, Casey DeSantis — a woman who, at one point, was considered a lock to succeed her husband, had she chosen to run.

It was not to be, and Tuesday just made it official. The Republican nominee for governor is Rep. Byron Donalds (R), the handpicked candidate of President Trump. And handpicked or not, Donalds may be sailing into some turbulent water. 

The first sign is that although Donalds won the primary, a majority of Republicans voted for other candidates. One reason was the devastating ads challenger Jay Collins ran against him — ads that Democrats will ensure have a second life from now until November.

I have spoken with numerous Republicans in Florida, and none wanted Donalds as the nominee. Not one. Is that indicative of how the election will go in November? Maybe not, but these are Republicans who desperately want to keep Florida red. 

Next is the victory by state Rep. Angie Nixon (D). Give her some props — Vindman and the entrenched Democratic Party outspent her about 16 to one, and she still humiliated him. But is her victory more about her strengths and connection with voters, or is it part of the growing voter dissatisfaction — and outright anger with incumbents — that we see sprouting up across the country? If it is the latter, which I believe it is, then that also spells trouble for Donalds and the Republican Party of Florida. 

Not only is Nixon the new, new thing but Donalds is part of the old, old thing — most especially for young voters, the working class, and non-white voters. Rising star or not, Nixon is going to bring out a bunch of new voters. And even if they may not be able to put her over the top against Republican incumbent Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Fla.), they will likely vote against Donalds while checking the box for Nixon.

It has been reported that there are 1.5 million more registered Republicans in Florida than Democrats. On paper, that seems to signal a slam-dunk for Donalds. But not so fast. A certain percentage of that 1.5 million identified as Republicans only because of support for DeSantis. Some share will stay home since DeSantis is not on the ballot in November. Some of them are angry with Trump for endorsing Donalds and not giving Casey DeSantis the proper time or respect to evaluate a potential run. Some share aren’t very impressed with Donalds, as the primary results demonstrate.

Nixon got more than 700,000 votes during the Democratic primary in deep red Florida.  Only a fool would underestimate her potential in the general. The promise of free stuff has worked since the invention of politics. Pardon the pun, but that promise will partially trump Trump and his various endorsements.

While not running against him, Nixon will still be an X factor in the eventual Donalds vote total — one that doesn’t even take into account Democratic primary winner for governor David Jolly, nor how much money the national party will pour into Florida. 

So did the Nixon victory “hand Republicans a November Gift”? Quite the opposite. I believe it has energized the Democratic base in the state while opening more eyes to the possibility that Florida is not as nearly as red as some have come to believe.

Donalds was mostly off the voter radar screen as a congressman. But now that he is the Republican nominee for governor, he is going to come under increased scrutiny. The betting odds may still list him as the favorite come November, but no one I know will be shocked if he goes down to defeat.

If I were the Republican leadership, I would cut out the personal attack nonsense and start addressing the issues that most matter to the working class.   

Douglas MacKinnon is a former White House and Pentagon official.

data.title: Cases of 'scromiting' condition tied to cannabis use spike among teens, young adults: New study
data.description:
(NEXSTAR) — The condition known to cause “scromiting” among some marijuana users has become more prevalent in the U.S., a recent report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention shows, though the trend among a specific age group may contradict previous understandings of the syndrome. 

Cannabis (or cannabinoid) hyperemesis syndrome (CHS) is as serious as it sounds. The condition, which can cause excessive vomiting with recurring bouts of severe stomach pain and nausea, was first detected in Australia two decades ago. Some have referred to a combination of CHS symptoms – screaming, due to the intense pain, and vomiting – as “scromiting.”

Hot showers and baths are often described as the only way to mitigate the discomfort. In rare cases, the condition has resulted in death, health officials said.

“[Patients] are not high in any fashion and in fact are in significant distress with uncontrolled vomiting, gagging, hurling, and pain,” Dr. Sam Torbati, the medical director of the Ruth and Harry Roman Emergency Department at Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles, explained to Nexstar via email. He sees patients already diagnosed with or presenting with suspected cases of cannabis hyperemesis arrive in his emergency department weekly. 

It’s not limited to his emergency department either. 

Virginia authorities reported that emergency department visits for CHS have jumped almost 29% since 2020. Significant spikes have also been reported in Massachusetts, Northern California, and parts of North Carolina. An official at Duke Regional Hospital in Durham, North Carolina, said last summer that patients with CHS are seen “every week, if not every day.” 

NOW PLAYING

In October, the World Health Organization added CHS to its diagnostic manual, a move meant to make it easier for health care providers to report the specific diagnosis rather than an overview of a patient’s symptoms. Patients may have otherwise been misdiagnosed as having another condition, like cyclic vomiting syndrome, according to a 2025 study. 

A new report from the CDC found that, as expected, emergency department visits involving CHS increased in the months after the WHO’s update. While researchers noted the rise “[suggests] improved recognition” of CHS, it could indicate that “the public health impact” of the condition was previously underestimated. 

The report also showed a concerning trend.

Younger age groups see spike in cases

Health experts have frequently described CHS as occurring in long-time, chronic cannabis users. A George Washington University study of more than 1,000 people who reported experiencing CHS found that over 40% said they used marijuana more than five times a day. Roughly the same proportion of people said they had regularly used marijuana for more than five years before experiencing CHS. 

However, the CDC’s latest report found “higher proportions” of emergency department visits involving CHS among younger persons. 

From January 2023 to September 2025, patients between the ages of 15 and 24 had the highest average proportion of monthly emergency department visits at nearly 10 per 10,000. After the diagnostic code for CHS was introduced back in October, the CDC found that the rate jumped to nearly 39 per 10,000. The next–highest age group, 25- to 34-year-olds, had a rate of 28 per 10,000.

For comparison, the national average rate was 3.19 per 10,000 between 2023 and 2025. It jumped to nearly 12 per 10,000 in the eight months after the WHO’s update, the CDC determined.

The increase in younger people diagnosed with the syndrome “was actually one of the surprising findings for us,” CDC’s Alana Vivolo-Kantor, the study’s first author, told The Associated Press.

“Because the assumption going in was, ‘well, how can they have chronic use?’” she said. “How early were they using cannabis?”

Researchers noted the trend, explaining that “emerging evidence indicates that symptom onset can occur much sooner than was previously estimated, including within the first year of cannabis use.”

The report theorized that, among younger people, there may be changes in cannabis use behavior, like starting at an earlier age and using “evolving methods of use” like vaping or higher-potency products. 

Torbati agreed. 

“Older data suggested CHS to occur after prolonged use but we are now seeing patients with CHS after only a few years of heavy cannabinoid use. This may be due to the higher potency of [marijuana] products which have much higher THC concentrations than in the past,” he said.

Recent studies had warned that younger people could be more at risk of experiencing CHS. 

A study out of Massachusetts found that younger adults, ages 18 to 34, could be at a higher risk of experiencing CHS, as could Hispanic and Black individuals. A similar 2025 study of nationwide data found CHS was most common among those ages 16 to 34 and corresponded with heavier cannabis use. The same study found CHS was “notably more prevalent in the South,” but that those who reported the highest rates of cannabis use were in states that have legalized recreational cannabis, which are primarily in other regions. 

Still, Torbati said that the condition impacts only a small proportion of people who use cannabis products. It’s also possible that a chronic user never develops CHS, health experts say. 

How does CHS present?

It’s not clear exactly how marijuana products cause CHS, though Cedars Sinai said it may be brought on by receptors in the brain no longer responding to marijuana as they had before. 

CHS can occur in three phases: prodromal, hyperemetic, and recovery. 

During the first, which “may last for months or years,” patients can experience belly pain and nausea in the morning. This may lead to increased marijuana use, as it is often used to treat such symptoms. 

In the hyperemetic phase, symptoms can become worse and progress to vomiting that is “overwhelming” and “recurrent,” lasting about a day or two. Patients may feel the need to bathe frequently, as hot water has been known to ease their nausea. It’s during this phase that health experts say patients typically seek medical care. 

During the final phase, recovery, symptoms fade over time before disappearing as the patient stops using any and all forms of cannabis. Symptoms are known to return if they try marijuana again, however. 

“[The] majority of patients have been diagnosed with CHS in the past and are either in denial or unable to stop use of marijuana products,” he explained. “These patients often will not provide accurate drug use histories, making the clinician’s job more challenging, often leading to unnecessary testing such as imaging with CT or ultrasound to rule out other conditions.”

They may further require “help from drug treatment specialists.” 

While there are treatment options to control the symptoms patients can experience, the “long term cure to this condition requires abstinence from cannabinoid products,” Torbati said. 

The CDC report, meanwhile, argued that there is a need to raise awareness of the condition among healthcare providers and the public, “but further education efforts might be needed to prevent the cause of CHS: cannabis use.”

Researchers also called for continued surveillance of the condition, “including the potential role of high-potency THC and hemp-derived products.”

If you believe you’re experiencing symptoms of CHS, health experts recommend speaking with your doctor.

data.title: Federal judge rules against Trump's 75-country visa ban
data.description:
A federal judge ruled against the Trump administration’s pause on issuing visas to immigrants from 75 countries on Friday. 

In a 61-page decision, U.S. District Judge Jeannette Vargas found that this policy was “contrary to law” and was “in excess” of Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s legal authority. 

The visa pause order was announced by the Trump administration in January as part of its efforts to curb an influx of immigrants they argued would place a strain on U.S. safety net programs. 

Vargas, who was nominated by former President Joe Biden, noted in her ruling that this ban affected nearly 40 percent of the world’s countries, including Egypt, Afghanistan, Somalia, Haiti, Iran, Brazil and Russia. 

“We are working to ensure the generosity of the American people will no longer be abused,” the State Department wrote in a social media post at the time of this announcement.  

In her Friday ruling, the federal judge cited the Immigration Nationality Act (INA) provision that “categorically prohibits” consular officers from basing their decisions in the visa review process on nationality. 

“Consular officers are required to conduct an individualized assessment of applicants and to refuse visas only to those whom the consular officer finds ineligible. The Policy nonetheless directs consular officers to refuse eligible applicants. 

Additionally, Vargas noted that the INA confers consular officers’ exclusive authority over the visa application review process. 

“Through the Policy, Secretary Rubio nonetheless overrides consular discretion and decision-making and dictates whether immigrant visas shall be granted or denied,” the judge wrote. “The Policy is thus patently unlawful and must be vacated under the [Administrative Procedure Act].”

The National Immigration Law Center, one of the groups representing the plaintiffs in this case, called the ruling a “significant victory” in a Friday statement. 

“The court made clear that immigration laws cannot be used to justify discrimination,” said Joanna Cuevas Ingram, a senior staff attorney at the organization. “We are determined to ensure every person and family this ban harmed receives appropriate relief and will continue to hold this administration accountable to its obligations under the law.” 

The Hill has reached out to the White House and the Justice Department for comment.

The ruling is the latest blow to the Trump administration’s efforts to crack down on immigration. In June, a federal judge ruled against the administration’s decision to bar the processing of any immigration application from 39 countries, stalling requests for work permits, green cards and citizenship applications.

data.title: The US is using the wrong measure of pressure on Iran
data.description:
Earlier this month — days after calling off a planned military strike against Iran due to a supposed diplomatic breakthrough — President Trump blasted Iran’s leadership on Truth Social as “unbelievably duplicitous.”

For weeks, Washington and Tehran have remained locked in a diplomatic stalemate, with little indication that either side is prepared to compromise. Around the same time, CNN reported that a senior officer at U.S. Central Command circulated an unusual request to military analysts for “creative and unconventional ways to pressure and punish Iran.” 

These developments are more closely connected than they appear. The request is more than simply a search for new instruments of pressure. It reflects a deeper strategic problem. The U.S. possesses overwhelming military, economic and diplomatic power. Yet those advantages matter only if they change how Tehran evaluates its options.

For years, Iran has approached confrontation with the U.S. from a simple assumption: Patience improves leverage. American administrations change. Elections reshape political priorities. Public attention shifts. Economic pressures accumulate. From Tehran’s perspective, delaying negotiations is not passive behavior — it is an active bargaining strategy. 

Unlike the Islamic Republic, every American administration operates within a visible political calendar. Midterm elections, fuel prices, congressional politics and public opinion inevitably shape Washington’s room for maneuver. Tehran studies that political calendar as carefully as it studies American force posture. Whether those factors ultimately determine U.S. policy is almost beside the point. What matters is that Iran believes they eventually will. 

This helps explain why successive American administrations have struggled to translate military superiority into durable political outcomes. Washington has often measured pressure by the tools it employs — airstrikes, sanctions, deployments and diplomatic isolation. Tehran has measured something else entirely, which is, whether each passing month improved its negotiating position. 

America’s regional partners further complicate that calculation. Saudi Arabia has reportedly urged restraint. Other Gulf states continue balancing two competing objectives of weakening Iran while avoiding a prolonged regional war that threatens their economies and domestic stability. From Tehran’s perspective, these competing interests reinforce an important expectation — that the coalition confronting Iran will eventually place greater value on stability than sustained pressure.

Conventional instruments remain indispensable. Military pressure, sanctions and diplomacy are not the problem. The problem is assuming that applying more pressure automatically produces greater leverage. Pressure succeeds only when it changes an adversary’s expectations. 

Thomas Schelling made this point decades ago in “Arms and Influence.” Coercion succeeds not because it imposes costs, but because it changes an adversary’s calculations. The relevant question today is therefore not how much damage American policy inflicts on Iran, but whether Tehran still believes that waiting promises a better outcome than negotiating today.

That distinction should reshape how Washington evaluates its strategy. Every military operation, diplomatic initiative, sanctions package or regional agreement should be judged against one strategic question: Does it strengthen or weaken Tehran’s confidence that delay improves its position? If the answer is no, tactical success is unlikely to translate into political success.

History offers reason to challenge Iran’s assumptions. The 1973 oil embargo did not permanently weaken the U.S. It accelerated American adaptation through greater energy resilience, technological innovation and strategic diversification. Democracies often appear vulnerable because their debates are public and their politics are noisy. Yet they have repeatedly demonstrated an ability to absorb shocks, adapt and emerge strategically stronger than their adversaries expected.

By confusing political debate for strategic weakness, Iran’s leaders may be making the same mistake that many of America’s adversaries have made before.

The ultimate measure of American strategy is neither the number of targets destroyed, nor the severity of sanctions imposed. It is whether Tehran concludes that further delay no longer improves its prospects. Military power creates opportunity. Coercion succeeds only when it changes expectations. 

Until Iran’s leaders believe that waiting no longer works to their advantage, Washington risks winning battles without achieving its strategic objective 

Bradley Martin is the executive director of the Near East Center for Strategic Studies. Dr. Liram Koblentz-Stenzler is the head of the Global Extremism and Antisemitism Desk at the International Institute for Counter-Terrorism at Reichman University, Herzliya, and a visiting scholar at Brandeis University.

data.title: Iran says 'world approved our victory' over the US
data.description:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Friday the war between the U.S. and Iran should end because the world has accepted Tehran’s victory in this conflict. 

His comments, which were reported by state media, come ahead of new economic sanctions from the U.S. expected next week. 

“The entire world approved our victory and the U.S. is hated,” he said, according to the state-run IRNA News Agency.

President Trump announced Wednesday that his administration would unleash the “most crushing economic operation ever” against Iran amid ongoing negotiations to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. 

“Oil smuggling, swap lines, cash transfers, exchange houses, ship registries, front companies — It all needs to stop NOW. You know who you are,” the president wrote in a Truth Social post.

“This will be an ECONOMIC D-DAY, and we need all of our Allies to stand with the United States of America to isolate, and defeat, the Iran threat,” Trump continued. 

The trading passage, which carries around a fifth of the world’s oil consumption on a daily basis during peacetime, has been effectively closed due to Iranian counterstrikes and a U.S. naval blockade. 

Iran and Oman have joint jurisdiction over this critical waterway, but Trump has threatened to make the strait a U.S. territory amid these ongoing talks. 

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is expected to unveil details of the new economic sanctions on Monday. 

“It is a one-two punch. We have ​the blockade, and we are going to have the toughest sanctions in history,” the secretary told ​CNBC on Thursday. “It is going to work in Iran and we are going to collapse this ⁠regime.”   

Iranian Foreign Affairs Minister Abbas Araghchi decried these anticipated economic penalties on Thursday, suggesting they were a means for the Trump administration to distract from domestic concerns about the cost of living.

“The so-called “Economic D-Day” is a diversion from America’s own crisis: unprecedented debt & surging interest costs,” the Iranian official wrote on social media. “Doubling down on failed policies will only bring further defeat—and enmity of Iranians. US economic terrorism threatens global economy and sovereignty worldwide.”

data.title: 'This is my place of business' — cakes and coffee in an age of rage
data.description:
“This is my place of business.”

Those words from Jim Sheehan, owner of the Wydaho Roasters coffee shop in Driggs, Idaho, have sparked the latest controversy over the right of businesses to refuse service on the basis of religious or political views.

Sheehan has drawn national attention after throwing out a group of pro-life teenagers, calling them the equivalent of a Ku Klux Klan meeting in his shop. Sheehan clearly caters to those who want their lattes with an added shot of rage.

However, this and a number of other cases have exposed the hypocrisy of many regarding the service businesses must provide customers with opposing views. From cakes to coffee, shops remain ground zero for an age of rage.

Years ago, politicians and pundits rallied around the effort to force Jack Phillips, a cakeshop owner, to create cakes celebrating same-sex marriages. Phillips objected that it violated his religious beliefs. The case went all the way to the Supreme Court in what many of us hoped would be a final resolution of this conflict.

I had long criticized the framing of the case (and other similar cases) under the religious clauses rather than treating it as a simple matter of free speech. In the end, the Supreme Court punted in a frustrating 2018 decision.

In 2023, however, the Supreme Court delivered a major victory for free speech in 303 Creative v. Elenis. It ruled that Lorie Smith, a Christian website designer, could refuse to provide services for a same-sex marriage. Justice Neil Gorsuch wrote that “the framers designed the Free Speech Clause of the First Amendment to protect the ‘freedom to think as you will and to speak as you think.’ … They did so because they saw the freedom of speech ‘both as an end and as a means.'”

But notably, in cases like Masterpiece Cakeshop, Phillips insisted that he would always sell cakes to any couple, including same-sex couples. He only refused to make cakes specifically celebrating same-sex marriages, due to his religious views.

The case of Wydaho is different. Sheehan refused the same general accommodation offered to all customers because he opposes pro-life causes. In the confrontation, Sheehan declared that “in my world” pro-lifers are no different from the Ku Klux Klan.

“This is my place of business,” he declared. “I did a lot of work to get people on the ballot so women would have the right to choose in the state of Idaho, and this is something I do not support, nor does my wife, and it’s our business. So we have that choice.”

In my view, they do have that choice. Yet it must also be acknowledged what Sheehan is doing is far more extreme than what Phillips did in Masterpiece Cakeshop. He is not being asked to create a coffee concoction opposing abortion, like a Cafe Au Life specialty drink. He acknowledges that other groups might use the shop — he just does not want these teenagers to use it to support pro-life causes.

The same controversy arose the same week across the country in Virginia. In Alexandria, Fatana Karimi, owner of the Karimi Salon, threw out a woman after she revealed that she was Israeli. Jessica Walton posted an account of the encounter, and a video was later posted on social media.

In the video, the person identified as Karimi says that she declared on Instagram that she would not serve those who support Israel. (She also adds that she got Walton to sign a release for the video.)

The Virginia Human Rights Act states that businesses cannot engage in “unlawful discrimination in employment because of race, color, religion, ethnic or national origin, sex, pregnancy, childbirth or related medical conditions, age, marital status, sexual orientation, gender identity, disability, or military status.” Karimi will likely argue she refused service not due to Walton’s religion or national origin, but due to her support for Israel — a political position.

The case is reminiscent of the abusive treatment afforded to Harvard Law Professor Alan Dershowitz at Martha’s Vineyard by a pierogi stand. He was also refused service over his political views.

The line between national origin and religious discrimination versus political discrimination can be tenuous and unclear. However, in the video, the owner states that it is her national identity that is causing the action: “Get out of my shop. I can’t provide service to an Israeli. It’s against my political beliefs. You need to leave immediately.”

Back in Idaho, Sheehan’s bizarre analogy to the KKK outraged many, to the point that he later apologized for it. However, it is fascinating that liberals are now celebrating the right to exclude others for political or religious reasons, even when they are not asked to engage in any expressive act or make any creative product that contravenes their beliefs.

If that is now the case, many owe individuals such as Phillips an apology for years of costly lawsuits, even after the Supreme Court gave him his first nominal victory.

Sheehan could be prosecuted if he were refusing general service or accommodations to the teenagers due to their race or religion. But he is refusing service on the basis of his own political views. Wydaho Roasters does not appear to want business from people who are pro-life, of whom there might be quite a few in Idaho. Karimi appears not to want either Israeli or possibly Jewish customers. It is a curious business plan to exclude such a large segment of the market, but some owners are sure to put their political views before their profits.

However, those on the left cannot have it both ways. They cannot reject the free speech rights of some owners to decline service while celebrating others’ refusal to do the same thing. None of this is likely to make society any more civil. No one wants a black eye to go with the red-eye espresso.

Of course, recognizing the free speech rights of an unhinged coffee shop owner does not require patronizing his establishment. Sheehan clearly does not want to serve pro-life citizens, and I expect the feeling is mutual.

Jonathan Turley is a law professor and the best-selling author of “Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution.” He is a member of the USA Today Board of Contributors.
